mainTopic: When to stop mentioning and requesting rain, the miracle year of rain in יואל's time, and רב נחמן's questions to רבי יצחק about puzzling פסוקים.
overview: The גמרא finishes the earlier question about mentioning rain. רבא and רב ששת rule that once you start mentioning rain on שמיני עצרת, you never stop. Even רב changed his mind to agree, and the הלכה follows this. A new משנה then asks until when we request rain: רבי יהודה says until פסח passes, and רבי מאיר says until ניסן ends, based on a פסוק in יואל about rain 'in the first month.' רב נחמן asks how the first rain (יורה) can be in ניסן when it normally falls in מרחשון. רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן that the פסוק describes one drought year in יואל's time. That year the people planted their last grain at the נביא's command, and the crop grew miraculously in eleven days, in time for the עומר. A פסוק in תהלים about sowing in tears and reaping with joy is explained as describing that generation. Then רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק a series of questions about hard פסוקים: what people ate in a seven-year famine, why God 'will not enter the city' (the ירושלים above waits for the ירושלים below), what 'one' sin burns the wicked (עבודה זרה), and why ירמיהו counts only 'two evils'. The answer to that last question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Once you start mentioning rain, you do not stop
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a different approach from the earlier view: once a person begins mentioning rain in davening, he keeps going without a break. רב ששת says the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Once a person has started mentioning rain, he does not stop. And רב ששת said the same: Once he has started, he does not stop.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own ruling on the earlier question: after you begin mentioning rain on שמיני עצרת, you keep mentioning it all winter with no break. רב ששת agrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier view held that in חוץ לארץ a person mentions rain on שמיני עצרת, then stops, and only starts again later. רבא rejects that back-and-forth: once the mention has begun, it continues without a pause. רב ששת adds the weight of a second אמורא saying the exact same words.

keyTerms.meaning: and so too said (another sage agrees)

phrases.english: Rava said:
Once he has started, he no longer stops.
phrases.notes: He means starting to mention rain in davening on שמיני עצרת.

phrases.english: And so too Rav Sheshet said:
Once he has started, he no longer stops.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִתְחִיל, שׁוּב אֵינוֹ פּוֹסֵק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative to the earlier 'start and stop' approach from the previous section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once one begins mentioning rain, he continues without interruption.

steps.title: Even רב changed his mind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רב himself took back his earlier 'start and stop' view. It quotes רב: count twenty-one days from ראש השנה, then begin mentioning rain and never stop.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even רב retracted, as רב חננאל said in the name of רב: One counts twenty-one days, the same way one counts ten days from ראש השנה to יום כיפור, and then he starts. Once he has started, he does not stop.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רבא's view: רב, who earlier held 'start and stop,' later changed his mind and also said 'once you start, you don't stop.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's new statement counts twenty-one days from ראש השנה, the same way one counts ten days to יום כיפור. After those twenty-one days you start mentioning rain, which means starting on שמיני עצרת. The key new point is the end of his statement: once you start, you do not stop. So the earlier 'start and stop' opinion has lost its main supporter.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב is adding a new waiting period after יום טוב. The twenty-one days are counted from ראש השנה, and the day right after them is שמיני עצרת, the usual starting day.

phrases.english: And even Rav retracted.
As Rav Ḥananel said that Rav said:
One counts twenty-one days
phrases.notes: Counted from ראש השנה. The twenty-first day is הושענא רבה, so the mention of rain starts the next day, שמיני עצרת.

phrases.english: just as one counts ten days
from Rosh HaShana until Yom Kippur,
and then he starts,
and once he has started, he no longer stops.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף רַב הֲדַר בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא and רב ששת by showing that רב himself came to agree with them.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that once one starts mentioning rain he does not stop.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב חננאל quoting רב's later statement.

steps.title: The final ruling: do not stop once you start
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that the הלכה follows the view that once you begin mentioning rain, you do not stop.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: once he has started, he does not stop.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the discussion with a practical ruling: once you start mentioning rain, keep going.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After רבא, רב ששת, and even רב all agree, the גמרא makes it official as the הלכה. The 'start and stop' approach is set aside in practice.
steps.whatToRemember: Once you begin saying משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם on שמיני עצרת, you keep saying it all winter without interruption. Even רב retracted his 'start and stop' view.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the practice everywhere, including חוץ לארץ, of mentioning rain from שמיני עצרת onward without stopping.

phrases.aramaic: וְהִלְכְתָא: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִתְחִיל, שׁוּב אֵינוֹ פּוֹסֵק.
phrases.english: And the halakha is: once he has started, he no longer stops.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִתְחִיל, שׁוּב אֵינוֹ פּוֹסֵק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the הלכה based on the views brought in steps 1 and 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה is that once one begins mentioning rain, he does not stop.

steps.title: משנה: until when do we request rain?
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה asks how long into the spring we keep requesting rain. רבי יהודה says until פסח has passed. רבי מאיר says until the end of ניסן, based on a פסוק in יואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Until when do we ask for rain? רבי יהודה says: until פסח has passed. רבי מאיר says: until ניסן is over, as it says: 'And He brings down rain for you, the first rain and the last rain, in the first month.'
steps.whatsHappening: The topic changes. The משנה now asks about the end of the rainy season: when do we stop asking for rain?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה ends the request when פסח is over. רבי מאיר extends it through all of ניסן. He brings a פסוק showing that rain can still fall in 'the first month,' which is ניסן, so all of ניסן still counts as rain season.
steps.confusionAlert: Requesting rain (שאלה, in ברך עלינו) is not the same as mentioning rain (הזכרה, in משיב הרוח). Steps 1-3 were about mentioning; this משנה is about requesting.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְנִי׳ עַד מָתַי שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים?
phrases.english: MISHNA: Until when does one request rain?

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: עַד שֶׁיַּעֲבוֹר הַפֶּסַח,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: Until Passover has passed,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: עַד שֶׁיֵּצֵא נִיסָן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: Until Nisan has ended,
as it is stated: “And He brings down rain for you,
the first rain and the last rain, in the first month.”
phrases.notes: יואל 2:23. 'The first month' is ניסן.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד מָתַי שׁוֹאֲלִין אֶת הַגְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה on a new question: when the request for rain ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: request rain until פסח passes. רבי מאיר: until ניסן ends, based on the פסוק in יואל.

steps.title: רב נחמן asks: isn't the first rain in מרחשון?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן challenges the פסוק רבי מאיר used: it seems to place the יורה (first rain) in ניסן, but a known teaching says the יורה falls in מרחשון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to רבי יצחק: The first rain in ניסן? The first rain is in מרחשון! As we learned: the first rain is in מרחשון and the last rain is in ניסן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by questioning the פסוק from the משנה. How can it say the first rain fell in ניסן, when the first rain normally comes in the fall?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to say both the first rain (מורה/יורה) and the last rain (מלקוש) come 'in the first month,' ניסן. But a ברייתא teaches that the first rain is in מרחשון and only the last rain is in ניסן. The פסוק seems to contradict the known order of the seasons.

keyTerms.meaning: the first rain of the season

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Naḥman said to Rabbi Yitzḥak:
The first rain in Nisan?
phrases.notes: The פסוק says מורה, and רב נחמן reads it as יורה, the first rain.

phrases.english: The first rain is in Marḥeshvan!
As we learned: The first rain is in Marḥeshvan
and the last rain is in Nisan!

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹרֶה בְּנִיסָן? יוֹרֶה בִּמְרַחְשְׁוָן הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the פסוק that רבי מאיר quoted in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The פסוק 'מורה ומלקוש בראשון' quoted in the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק seems to place the first rain in ניסן, but a ברייתא teaches that the first rain falls in מרחשון.

steps.title: The פסוק describes one unusual year in יואל's time
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן: the פסוק describes a specific year in the days of יואל, during a terrible locust plague, when no rain fell all winter and the first rain only came on the first of ניסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: In the days of יואל בן פתואל this פסוק came true, in the time about which it is written: 'What the גזם left, the ארבה ate...' That year, אדר ended and no rain had fallen. The first rainfall came down for them on the first of ניסן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers רב נחמן's question by explaining that the פסוק is not describing a normal year but a special year of drought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the first rain comes in מרחשון, just as the ברייתא says. But in יואל's time, during a disastrous locust plague, the whole winter passed with no rain, so the 'first rain' only arrived on ראש חודש ניסן. So the פסוק and the ברייתא do not contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: the first rainfall of the season

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
In the days of Joel, son of Pethuel,
this verse was fulfilled,

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״יֶתֶר הַגָּזָם אָכַל הָאַרְבֶּה וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: about which it is written: “That which the palmer-worm left, the locust has eaten, etc.”
phrases.notes: יואל 1:4

phrases.english: That year, Adar ended
and no rain had fallen;
the first rainfall came down for them
on the first of Nisan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב נחמן's question about the first rain being in ניסן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the פסוק to a specific historical event.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seems to describe the normal yearly pattern, placing the first rain in ניסן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק describes one unusual drought year in יואל's time, when the first rain fell on the first of ניסן. Normally the first rain is in מרחשון.

steps.title: The prophet tells the starving people to plant anyway
steps.stepSummary: After the late first rain, the נביא tells ישראל to sow. They ask whether they should plant their last bit of food and starve. He tells them to plant anyway, and a miracle reveals hidden grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: The נביא said to ישראל: Go out and plant! They said to him: Someone who has only a little wheat or barley left, should he eat it and live, or plant it and die? He said: Even so, go out and plant. A miracle happened, and they found grain hidden in the walls and in ant holes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps telling the story of the locust year from Step 6. Now it describes what happened right after that late first rain on the first of ניסן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people's question makes sense: planting this late looked hopeless, and eating the last grain would at least keep them alive a little longer. The נביא insists they plant, and a miracle provides extra seed from hidden places.

keyTerms.meaning: A small measure of dry food
Ant holes, where ants store grain

phrases.english: The prophet said to Israel:
Go out and sow!
They said to him: One who has
one kav of wheat or two kavs of barley,
phrases.notes: A קַב is a small amount of food.

phrases.english: should he eat it and live,
or sow it and die?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן
phrases.english: He said to them: Even so,
go out and sow.
A miracle was done for them,
and what was in the walls was revealed to them
phrases.notes: He means grain that was hidden away inside the walls.

phrases.english: and what was in the ant holes.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם נָבִיא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל: צְאוּ וְזִרְעוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the locust year that רבי יצחק used in Step 6 to answer רב נחמן's challenge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Following the נביא's command, the people sowed despite their hunger, and a miracle supplied hidden grain.

steps.title: The crop grows in eleven days and the עומר is brought on time
steps.stepSummary: They plant on the second to fourth of ניסן, the second rain falls on the fifth, and by the sixteenth the grain is ready for the עומר. Grain that normally needs six months grew in eleven days.
steps.simpleTranslation: They went out and planted on the second, third, and fourth of ניסן, and the second rain fell on the fifth of ניסן. They brought the עומר on the sixteenth of ניסן. So grain that normally takes six months to grow grew in eleven days, and the עומר, normally brought from six-month grain, was brought from eleven-day grain.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches its high point: the crop grew miraculously fast. The גמרא counts the days to show how amazing it was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The עומר has to be brought on the sixteenth of ניסן from the new crop. Counting from the fifth (when the second rain fell) to the sixteenth gives eleven days, compared to the usual six months of growth.

keyTerms.meaning: A rainfall that soaks the ground
The barley offering from the new crop, brought on the sixteenth of ניסן

phrases.english: They went out and sowed
on the second, third, and fourth,
phrases.notes: These are days of ניסן, right after the first rain on the first of the month.

phrases.english: and the second rainfall came down for them
on the fifth of Nisan.
They offered the omer on the sixteenth of Nisan;
it turns out that grain which grows in six months
grew in eleven days.
It turns out that the omer, which is offered
from grain of six months,

phrases.aramaic: קָרֵב מִתְּבוּאָה שֶׁל אַחַד עָשָׂר יוֹם.
phrases.english: was offered from grain of eleven days.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָצְאוּ וְזָרְעוּ שֵׁנִי וּשְׁלִישִׁי וּרְבִיעִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: after planting, the second rain comes and the crop grows miraculously fast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: That year the עומר was brought on time from grain that grew in only eleven days.
steps.whatToRemember: In the year of יואל, the first rain came on the first of ניסן, the second on the fifth, and the עומר was still brought on the sixteenth from eleven-day grain.

steps.title: A פסוק in תהלים describes that generation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא applies the פסוק 'Those who sow in tears will reap with joy' to the generation of יואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And about that generation the verse says: 'Those who sow in tears will reap with joy. He goes along weeping, carrying the bag of seed, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from תהלים and says it is talking about this exact generation. This also sets up the next questions about what the פסוק's words mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people planted in tears, afraid of starving, and then harvested with joy when the crop grew miraculously. The פסוק fits their story closely.

phrases.english: And about that generation it says:
"Those who sow in tears will reap with joy.
phrases.notes: תהלים 126:5

phrases.english: He goes along weeping,
carrying the bag of seed, etc."
phrases.notes: תהלים 126:6

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל אוֹתוֹ הַדּוֹר הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects the story just told to a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.raayaObject: The story of sowing in hunger and reaping with joy in the days of יואל

steps.title: What does 'he goes along weeping' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the words 'he goes along weeping, carrying the bag of seed' mean.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of 'He goes along weeping, carrying the bag, etc.'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what this part of the פסוק means. It is setting up רבי יהודה's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to describe both weeping and joy for the same person. The גמרא wants to know who is weeping and how that fits the story.

keyTerms.meaning: The bag or measure of seed

phrases.english: What is "He goes along weeping,
carrying the bag, etc."?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״הָלוֹךְ יֵלֵךְ וּבָכֹה נֹשֵׂא מֶשֶׁךְ וְגוֹ׳״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a phrase in the פסוק just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to understand 'he goes along weeping' in the setting of that generation

steps.title: רבי יהודה: the ox cries while plowing and eats on the way back
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה explains that the ox cried as it plowed, but on the way back it was already eating new sprouts from the furrow. That is the 'coming with joy.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: An ox, when it plowed, went along crying, but on its way back it ate young sprouts from the furrow. And this is: 'He will surely come with joy.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה answers the question: the one weeping is the plowing ox. By the time it turned back down the row, the seeds had already sprouted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows how fast the crop grew: in the time it took to plow a row and come back, the grain had already started growing. So the weeping and the joy happened almost at once.

keyTerms.meaning: A furrow, the row cut by a plow

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said:
An ox, when it plows,
goes along crying,
and on its way back
eats young shoots from the furrow.
And this is: "He will surely come with joy."
phrases.notes: This is the next part of the same פסוק, תהלים 126:6.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: שׁוֹר, כְּשֶׁהוּא חוֹרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The weeping one is the plowing ox; on its return trip it already eats new sprouts, which is the 'coming with joy.'

steps.title: What does 'carrying his sheaves' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the end of the פסוק: 'carrying his sheaves.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of 'carrying his sheaves'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about another phrase in the same פסוק. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to know what was special about the sheaves of that miracle harvest.

phrases.english: What is "carrying his sheaves"?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״נֹשֵׂא אֲלֻמֹּתָיו״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second question on the same פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What was special about the sheaves of that harvest

steps.title: רב חסדא: the grain head was twice as long as the stalk
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא (or a ברייתא) explains that the stalk was one span long and the head of grain was two spans.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said, and some say it was taught in a ברייתא: The stalk was one span, and the head of grain was two spans.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the sheaves were special because the grain heads were huge compared to the stalks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the stalk is much longer than the head of grain. That year the head was twice the length of the stalk, so the sheaves were heavy and full, a sign of great blessing.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה
A span, from thumb to pinky of a spread hand

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said,
and some say it was taught in a baraita:
The stalk was a span,
the ear was two spans.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ בְּמַתְנִיתָא תָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The sheaves were remarkable: the stalk was one span and the grain head two spans.
steps.whatToRemember: The whole story explains why the פסוק in יואל places the first rain in ניסן: it describes one miracle year, when the late rains still produced a great harvest.

steps.title: What did they eat during the seven-year famine?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק what people ate during the seven years of famine mentioned in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to רבי יצחק: The פסוק says, 'For God has called for a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years.' What did people eat during those seven years?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new set of questions from רב נחמן to רבי יצחק. This first one asks how people survived a seven-year famine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic of famine connects to the earlier steps about hunger and plenty in the days of יואל. The question is practical: seven years is a very long time to go without food, so what was there to eat?

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written? (an opening for explaining a פסוק)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"For the Lord has called for a famine
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 8:1

phrases.aramaic: וְגַם בָּא אֶל הָאָרֶץ שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים״,
phrases.english: and it will also come upon the land for seven years"?
In those seven years, what did they eat?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the famine of יואל's time to a related פסוק about a seven-year famine.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How people fed themselves through seven full years of famine.

steps.title: The famine got worse each year
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן that each year people were forced to eat something worse, until in the seventh year they ate their own arms.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: רבי יוחנן said this. In year one they ate what was stored in their houses. In year two they ate what was left in the fields. In year three, kosher animals. In year four, non-kosher animals. In year five, bugs and creeping creatures. In year six, their own sons and daughters. In year seven, the flesh of their own arms, which fulfills the פסוק, 'Each man will eat the flesh of his own arm.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers the question with a year-by-year list from רבי יוחנן. Each year the food grows more desperate and terrible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer shows how a long famine slowly strips away everything. First people use up their stored food, then their animals, then forbidden creatures, and finally they reach horrors. The last stage is tied to a פסוק in ישעיה, so the list ends by showing that this פסוק came true.

keyTerms.meaning: Repulsive creatures and creeping things, like bugs
To fulfill what is said (shows a פסוק came true)

steps.whatToRemember: The seven years of famine went from stored food, to field crops, to kosher animals, to non-kosher animals, to bugs, to children, to their own arms.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
The first year they ate what was in the houses;
the second year they ate what was in the fields;
the third year, the meat of kosher animals;
the fourth year, the meat of non-kosher animals;
the fifth year, the meat of repulsive and creeping creatures;
the sixth year, the flesh of their sons and daughters;
the seventh year, the flesh of their own arms,
to fulfill what is said:
"Each man shall eat the flesh of his own arm."
phrases.notes: ישעיה 9:19

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A year-by-year list of what people ate, ending with the fulfillment of the פסוק in ישעיה.

steps.title: A puzzling verse: 'I will not enter the city'
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks about the פסוק in הושע. Why would God not enter the city just because there is holiness among the people?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן also asked רבי יצחק: The פסוק says, 'Holy in your midst, and I will not enter the city.' Does this mean that because there is holiness among you, God will not come into the city? That makes no sense.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן asks a second question, this time about a פסוק that seems to say something strange.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the פסוק seems to say that holiness among the people is the reason God stays out of the city. That is backwards: holiness should bring God in, not keep Him away. So רב נחמן wants to know how to read it correctly.

keyTerms.meaning: I will not enter the city

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"Holy in your midst, and I will not enter the city"?
phrases.notes: הושע 11:9

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דִּבְקִרְבְּךָ קָדוֹשׁ לֹא אָבוֹא בְּעִיר?
phrases.english: Because there is holiness in your midst, I will not enter the city?

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate question from the same pair of אמוראים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to make sense of a פסוק that seems to say holiness keeps God away from the city.

steps.title: God waits to enter the heavenly ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן: הקדוש ברוך הוא said He will not enter the ירושלים above until He enters the ירושלים below.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: רבי יוחנן said this. הקדוש ברוך הוא said: I will not enter the ירושלים that is up above until I enter the ירושלים down below.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק explains the hard פסוק by saying 'the city' means the heavenly ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reading changes what 'the city' refers to. 'Holy in your midst' means the earthly ירושלים once it is holy again. Until that happens, God 'will not enter the city' above. So the holiness down below is the condition for God entering the city above, not the reason He stays out.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He (God)

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches that what happens in the earthly ירושלים matters even in heaven. God is pictured as waiting for the earthly city to be rebuilt.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
I will not enter the Jerusalem above
until I enter the Jerusalem below!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16 by reading 'the city' as the heavenly ירושלים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק means God will not enter the heavenly ירושלים until the earthly ירושלים is holy and He enters it.

steps.title: Is there really a ירושלים above?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether such a place as a heavenly ירושלים really exists.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there really a ירושלים up above?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the idea the answer just relied on: a ירושלים in heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 17 only works if there are two ירושלים, one above and one below. The גמרא wants a source showing that a heavenly ירושלים really exists.

keyTerms.meaning: And is there really...? (questions whether something exists)

phrases.english: And is there really a Jerusalem above?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the idea that the answer in step 17 depends on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that a heavenly ירושלים exists.

steps.title: Yes, there is, as a verse shows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes, and proves it from a פסוק in תהלים that describes ירושלים as a city 'joined together.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. The פסוק says: 'ירושלים, built up like a city that is joined together.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a ירושלים above does exist, and brings a פסוק as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'joined together' suggest that ירושלים is linked with something like itself. The גמרא reads this as two ירושלים, the one above and the one below, bound together. This supports רבי יוחנן's reading from step 17.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two ירושלים, one in heaven and one on earth, and they are linked. God will not enter the one above until He enters the one below.

phrases.english: Yes, as it is written:
"Jerusalem, built up like a city
phrases.notes: תהלים 122:3

phrases.english: that is joined together."
phrases.notes: 'Joined together' is read as hinting at two ירושלים, one above and one below, linked to each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 with a פסוק that proves a ירושלים above exists.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. The phrase 'joined together' in תהלים shows that ירושלים has a twin above that is linked to it.

steps.title: What does 'with one they are brutish' mean?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק to explain the פסוק in ירמיהו: 'And with one they are brutish and foolish.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to רבי יצחק: What does the פסוק mean, 'And with one they are brutish and foolish, the teaching of their vanity is a stock'?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן asks another question about a פסוק, just like he did before. This sets up the next answer from רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'with one' but does not say one what. The word יבערו can mean 'brutish,' but it can also mean 'burn.' That opening will drive the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written?
They are brutish, or they burn

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"And with one they are brutish and foolish,
phrases.notes: יבערו can also mean "they burn." Keep that in mind, because the answer reads it that way.

phrases.english: the teaching of their vanity is a stock [of wood]"?
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 10:8

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the same chain of רב נחמן's questions to רבי יצחק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the 'one' thing the פסוק refers to?

steps.title: The one sin that burns the wicked is idol worship
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers in the name of רבי יוחנן: there is one sin that burns the wicked in גיהנם, and that sin is עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: There is one sin that makes the wicked burn in גיהנם. What is it? עבודה זרה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers by reading יבערו as 'burn': the 'one' thing is a single sin that burns the wicked in גיהנם. He names it as עבודה זרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'one' now means one especially severe sin. Reading יבערו as 'burn' turns the פסוק into a statement about punishment in גיהנם. The proof that this sin is עבודה זרה comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: גיהנם, the place of punishment for the wicked

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
There is one [sin] that burns the wicked in Gehinnom.
What is it? Idol worship.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'one' is a single sin that burns the wicked in גיהנם, which is עבודה זרה.

steps.title: Proof from the shared word 'vanity'
steps.stepSummary: The proof that the sin is עבודה זרה: the same word הבל (vanity) appears in our פסוק and in a פסוק about idols.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here, 'the teaching of their vanity is a stock,' and it says there about idols, 'They are vanity, a work of delusion.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן proves that the sin is עבודה זרה by matching a word that appears in two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים use the word הבל. The second פסוק is clearly about idols, so the 'vanity' in our פסוק must also mean idols. That is how we know the 'one' sin is עבודה זרה.
steps.whatToRemember: The 'one' sin that burns the wicked in גיהנם is עבודה זרה, proven by the word הבל that appears in both פסוקים.

phrases.english: It is written here:
"The teaching of their vanity is a stock,"
and it is written there:
"They are vanity, a work of delusion."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 10:15. This פסוק is talking about idols.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּתִיב הָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the identification made in step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That the 'one' sin is עבודה זרה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word הבל in ירמיהו 10:8 matches הבל in ירמיהו 10:15, which is about idols.

steps.title: Only two evils? What about the twenty-four?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks about ירמיהו's words 'my people have done two evils.' Were there really only two? Were the twenty-four sins listed elsewhere ignored?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to רבי יצחק: What does the פסוק mean, 'For my people have done two evils'? Were there only two? Were the twenty-four left aside for them?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן asks a new question about a different פסוק. He points out that it seems to undercount the people's sins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the people did 'two evils,' but elsewhere twenty-four sins are listed. So why does this פסוק mention only two? Were the other sins forgiven?

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי דִּכְתִיב: ״כִּי שְׁתַּיִם רָעוֹת עָשָׂה עַמִּי״,
phrases.english: What is the meaning of what is written: "For my people have done two evils"?
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 2:13

phrases.english: Were there only two?
Were the twenty-four left aside for them?
phrases.notes: He means the twenty-four sins listed in יחזקאל. Were those simply let go?

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the same chain, about a different פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the פסוק count only two evils when twenty-four sins are listed elsewhere?
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Twenty-four sins are listed elsewhere, so saying 'two' seems to leave the rest out.

steps.title: The answer begins: one sin that is
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק starts to answer in the name of רבי יוחנן: there is one sin that is... The sentence continues on the next part of the daf.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רבי יוחנן said: One sin that is...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק begins his answer to the 'two evils' question. The answer is cut off here and continues next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once again רבי יוחנן's answer opens by pointing to one particular sin ('אחת שהיא'). How this explains why the פסוק counts only 'two' is finished on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the end of the answer here. The sentence stops in the middle and finishes on the next part of the daf.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
One [sin] that is...

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer begins by describing one particular sin. It is completed in the next part of the daf.
